topic: servicing a vintage farm tractor before the ploughing season

provenance.author: glowny-en-c
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a parts and hours sheet for the same service with closed task questions, base is a diagnostic talk about hard starting and grey smoke. Grounded external referent: the fuel pump, introduced in turn 0 (weeping seam) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (diaphragm, seam, kit fitting, sludge at the feed).

a: The tractor service needs a parts order and the fluids come first on the sheet.
The engine oil takes eight litres and the gearbox oil takes twelve litres.
The back axle takes six litres of the same grade as the gearbox.
Work out the total litres of oil across the three fills in one figure.
How many five litre cans does that total need if cans may not be split?
base: Our old tractor has to plough eight acres next month and it starts harder every week.
It was my grandfather's machine and it has never missed a season on this farm.
The fuel pump weeps a little at the seam and the filter bowl shows black flakes.
Once running it pulls well, though it blows grey smoke on a cold morning.
Where should a winter service start so the ploughing does not catch us out?

a: The three fills add to twenty-six litres of oil across engine, gearbox, and axle.
Twenty-six litres needs six five litre cans with four litres left in hand.
The filters on the list are oil, fuel, and air at one of each.
The fuel line kit adds two metres of pipe and four clips to the order.
Which count of cans goes on the order line beside the oil grade?
base: Start with the fuel side, because flakes in the bowl mean the tank is shedding rust.
Drain a cupful from the tank tap and let it settle in a glass jar.
Hard starting like yours often begins at the pump, whose diaphragm hardens with age.
At cranking speed a tired pump starves the engine before the first fire.
Does the smoke clear once the engine warms, or does it hang about all day?

a: Six cans go on the order line beside the thirty grade oil for the season.
Now price the whole order using the list the parts man read out this morning.
The oil is nine pounds a can and the filter set is twenty-two pounds.
The fuel line kit is eight pounds and the diaphragm kit is fourteen pounds.
What do the four lines come to when they are added as one figure?
base: The jar test showed a red brown layer on the bottom by the next morning.
The smoke clears after ten minutes and the engine then runs sweet all day.
The pump seam weeps more when the tank is full than when it runs low.
There is a spare diaphragm kit in the barn from a parts sale years ago.
Would an old rubber kit from the barn shelf still be safe to fit?

a: The four lines come to ninety-eight pounds as one figure on the order sheet.
Next set out the service jobs across the two Saturdays in plain working order.
Saturday one holds the fuel work, meaning tank drain, pump kit, and the new lines.
Saturday two holds the three oil changes and the two other filters in one run.
How many separate jobs sit on Saturday one as the list now stands?
base: Rubber ages on the shelf as surely as on the tractor, just more slowly.
Check the kit, and if the diaphragm folds without cracking and smells of rubber, it will serve.
Fit it to the pump with the mark at twelve and snug the screws evenly.
While the pump is open, rinse the sediment bowl and blow the feed pipe through.
Is there a tap on the tank low enough to drain the rust right out?

a: Saturday one carries three separate jobs as the list now stands on the sheet.
One correction has come from the barn before the day plan is written out fully.
The gearbox oil fill is fourteen litres, not twelve as it was first read out.
Rework the total litres and the can count on the five litre rule.
How many cans does the order need now and what is left spare?
base: There is a drain plug under the tank, though it has not moved in my lifetime.
I soaked it in penetrating oil overnight and it finally gave this morning.
With the tank empty I can see the pump feed sitting in a well of sludge.
The old fuel that came out looks like tea and smells sour in the can.
Should the tank come off for a proper clean or will a rinse do?

a: The new oil total comes to twenty-eight litres across the three fills together.
Twenty-eight litres still needs six cans with two litres left spare in hand.
The order cost stays at ninety-eight pounds because the cans did not change.
Now set out the day times using two hours as the span for each single job.
How many hours does Saturday one hold at three jobs of two hours each?
base: Take the tank off, because sour fuel leaves a varnish a rinse will never shift.
Slosh it with clean diesel and a handful of gravel, then rinse and dry it.
Let the pump stand dry while the tank is away, with a rag over its inlet.
Refit with the new lines and clips, and bin every one of the old ones.
Is there a second pair of hands about when the tank comes off its cradle?

a: Saturday one holds six hours of work at three jobs of two hours each time.
Saturday two holds the four remaining jobs on the same two hour span as before.
Add one hour of parts fetching to each Saturday before the totals go down on paper.
Give the full hours for each Saturday and then for the whole service.
Which Saturday carries the longer day when the fetching hour is counted in?
base: My son can lift with me on Sunday, so the tank comes off then.
While it dries I want to look at the smoke, since the pump work may not cure it.
Grey smoke on cold mornings has been with us for two or three winters now.
The old man always said the engine was cold blooded and left it at that.
Could the smoke be nothing more than a tired old thermostat holding the engine cold?

a: Saturday one comes to seven hours when the fetching hour is counted in.
Saturday two comes to nine hours on the same rule and is the longer day.
The whole service stands at sixteen hours across the two Saturdays together.
Now list the parts total, the oil total, and the hours on one closing line.
Does the closing line read ninety-eight pounds, twenty-eight litres, and sixteen hours?
base: A stuck thermostat is a fine suspect, and it is cheap to prove either way.
Warm the engine and feel the top hose, which should stay cool then heat quickly.
If the hose warms straight away, the thermostat is open and the engine runs cold.
A cold running engine smokes grey and wears its bores faster than a warm one.
While you are in there, does the radiator hold pressure on its old cap?

a: The closing line reads as it was stated and goes onto the sheet without change.
Now add the thermostat at six pounds and the cap at four pounds to the order.
Rework the whole order total with those two lines counted in as one figure.
Set the fitting time at one extra hour on the second Saturday plan.
Write the new order total and the new hours total on the closing line.
base: The top hose warmed straight away, so the thermostat has been open for years.
There is a new thermostat and a cap on the shelf beside the diaphragm kit.
My son found the receipt, and the old man had bought them the winter he fell ill.
We will fit them on the second Saturday and think of him while we do it.
The ploughing match is set for the last weekend of next month.

a: The order total moves to one hundred eight pounds with the two new lines.
The hours move to seventeen with the fitting hour on the second Saturday.
The closing line reads one hundred eight pounds, twenty-eight litres, and seventeen hours.
The plan holds two Saturdays, seven jobs, and one steady hour of running after.
The sheet closes with the far field ploughing set for the last weekend.
base: Fitting his parts for the match is the kind of service no manual ever lists.
With clean fuel, a fresh diaphragm, and a warm engine, the starting should come easy.
Run the tractor for an hour after the second Saturday and watch the filter bowl.
If the bowl stays clean through that hour, the tank work has done its job.
Plough the far field steady, and the old machine will not let you down.
